meta.title: ROHACELL Qualification Radar
meta.scope: Europe & UK — eVTOL / AAM / cargo UAV and tactical defence UAS

briefs.headline: Baseline scan — 28 companies screened, 7 in Tier A.
briefs.summary: First full sweep of European and UK eVTOL, cargo UAV and defence drone makers. Tekever ranks first: AR6 enters production at Swindon by end-2026 using autoclave-cured carbon prepreg, so core selection is live now.

briefs.headline: Sectors widened beyond drones — motorsport & automotive and rail, marine & wind seeded.
briefs.summary: Eight seed entries added across two new sectors. The honest headline: motorsport carries real PMI opportunity (Dash-CAE monocoque, Permali as a two-sector channel), while wind and marine are cost-driven markets already owned by PET, balsa and SAN foam — logged mainly so the daily scan can spot the rare high-performance exception. Two entries are competitors rather than customers, and are marked as such.

briefs.headline: Widened from drones to nine markets — space, medical, sports, RF, certified aircraft and industrial added.
briefs.summary: Thirteen seed entries across six new sectors. The strongest additions are EnduroSat and Aerospacelab in space, where satellite structures are almost entirely sandwich panel and both are scaling production, and SHD Composites as a prepreg channel partner. Medical imaging is included because radiolucent PMI is already the incumbent there — that sector is about defending a position rather than winning one. Three entries are honest sector watches with no company named yet: radomes, hydrogen aircraft and industrial robotics. Orbex is logged as dead after its February 2026 collapse, so nobody works a name that no longer exists.

briefs.headline: Research mining added — patents, papers and EU-funded projects now scanned alongside the news.
briefs.summary: New Research signals section. A company that publishes a paper or files a patent naming ROHACELL has already had the material in a lab, which makes it a warmer lead than anything a funding announcement produces. The first sweep found the Clean Aviation third call — twelve EU projects starting in 2026 with published partner lists, including CRYOSTAR on composite cryogenic hydrogen tanks. Ascendance Flight Technologies was surfaced this way rather than through the news. Also logged: Fraunhofer work on thermoplastic sandwich rudders, which is a competitive threat rather than an opportunity, and an independent three-way core comparison paper worth reading before technical meetings.

briefs.headline: Public-use sweep widened to indexed social posts — a Formula SAE team confirmed as a ROHACELL user.
briefs.summary: Instagram hashtag pages are login-walled and cannot be browsed, but individual posts are indexed by search engines and can be found that way. Doing so turned up Unicamp E-Racing in Brazil, whose Formula SAE car uses ROHACELL in the front wing, rear wing and endplates — confirmed by Evonik’s own release. This corrects the earlier conclusion that no student team could be confirmed. Also found AMT Composites in South Africa, plus Epic Fibers and Composite Envisions selling finished carbon/ROHACELL panels.

briefs.headline: Research tab filled out — 18 publications, NASA reports, supply news and a stealth paper worth reading.
briefs.summary: Deep publication sweep across journals, NASA NTRS, patents and Evonik supply announcements. The standout is a 2025 paper on rigid PMI composite foam for electromagnetic dissipation and infrared stealth — it moves PMI from a structural core that happens to be RF-transparent to a functional stealth material, which is directly relevant to the open radome and RF gap. Also logged: a bead-based route to complex-shaped PMI that could change the cost argument, thermo-mechanical failure data useful at Destinus, and both Evonik capacity expansions, which answer the lead-time and single-site objections that usually kill core qualification.

briefs.headline: Trade shows added — exhibitor lists as a pre-qualified source of targets.
briefs.summary: New Shows tab covering Advanced Engineering UK (4–5 November 2026, NEC Birmingham), Space Tech Expo Europe (November 2026, Bremen) and JEC World (March 2027, Paris). Advanced Engineering is the near-term one at about eleven weeks out, and several already-tracked companies exhibit there. The daily scan now watches for exhibitor lists as they publish and cross-checks them against the tracked list, adding new names and flagging existing ones as worth meeting.

briefs.headline: Trade show calendar rebuilt properly — 12 shows across all nine markets, correcting a thin first attempt.
briefs.summary: The first version listed only three shows and missed obvious ones, including DroneX at ExCeL London on 29–30 September — six weeks away, in the UK, and squarely in the top market. That was a poor first pass and is now corrected. The calendar covers all nine markets with organiser-confirmed dates where available and honest "dates to confirm" flags where not. Near-term order: DroneX (29–30 Sep), Advanced Engineering UK (4–5 Nov, NEC), Space Tech Expo Europe (17–19 Nov, Bremen). JEC World is confirmed for 2–4 March 2027 and AERO Friedrichshafen for 14–17 April 2027. Shows judged low-value — METSTRADE and ISPO — are listed with the reason rather than omitted.

companies.name: Tekever
companies.platform: AR3 / AR5 / AR6 heavy-lift (700 kg MTOW, 200 kg payload)
companies.what: AR6 heavy-lift UAV — 700 kg max take-off weight, 200 kg payload, roughly 500 km range. AR3 and AR5 already in service.
companies.where: Portuguese-owned; the site that matters is Swindon, Wiltshire — their fourth and largest UK facility. Also Southampton and Portugal.
companies.opp: The single best opportunity on this list. AR6 goes into production at Swindon by the end of 2026, so the core material for a brand-new 700 kg airframe is being chosen right now. CompositesWorld confirms autoclave-cured carbon prepreg for wings and fuselage — exactly the process where PMI wins. It sits inside a £400M expansion programme called OVERMATCH, so the volumes are real.
companies.ask: Head of Composites / Materials & Processes at the Swindon manufacturing hub. Lead with autoclave compatibility and the aerospace qualification data package.
companies.materials: Confirmed: autoclave-cured carbon prepreg wings/fuselage, glass for RF-transparent parts, aramid for impact

events.text: AR6 production launches end-2026 at Swindon hub; partnership with iCOMAT for rate composites

companies.name: Vertical Aerospace
companies.platform: VX4 / Valo
companies.what: VX4 and the new Valo electric air taxi. Carbon composite airframe, certified aircraft.
companies.opp: Valo certification has slipped to 2029 — bad for them, good for you. The design and supply chain are still open, and they raised roughly $100M in August 2026 to fund the certification push. Certified programmes buy on traceable allowables and qualification data far more than on unit price, which plays to Rohacell's strength over cheaper foams.
companies.ask: Materials & Processes or Structures Engineering. Lead with the qualification data package and certification support, not price.

events.text: Valo certification pushed to 2029 — design and supply chain still open; fresh cash for cert programme

companies.platform: Rapid Tow Shearing structures for Tekever AR6 and others
companies.what: Tier composites supplier, not an aircraft maker. Rapid Tow Shearing / steered-fibre structures, including structures for Tekever's AR6.
companies.opp: A back-door into several aircraft programmes at once. Because they supply structures to multiple OEMs, one qualification here carries Rohacell into programmes you never have to sell individually. NATO Innovation Fund backed and scaling alongside Tekever. Lower resistance than an OEM, and they speak your technical language.

events.text: Not an OEM — a route into several OEM programmes at once

companies.platform: Long-range strike, jet UAVs, counter-drone (Thales partnership Jul 2026)
companies.what: Long-range strike drones and high-speed jet UAVs. Partnered with Thales on counter-drone and long-range strike in July 2026.
companies.where: Switzerland (HQ), with operations in Germany and Spain.
companies.opp: Your strongest technical argument sits here. High-speed airframes run hot, and elevated service temperature is where PMI beats PET and PVC foam outright rather than competing on price. Reportedly raising €200M at a €5B valuation, so budget is not the constraint. A performance sell, not a cost sell.

companies.opp: Raised $1.2 billion at an $8 billion valuation in July 2026 — the largest European defence-tech round to date — and scaling from hundreds to thousands of airframes a year. Because they are selling the tub to multiple car makers, qualifying once here puts PMI into every vehicle that adopts it — the same channel logic as iCOMAT in aerospace.

research.title: Clean Aviation third call — 12 projects, €945M, starting 2026
research.summary: Twelve new EU-funded aviation projects begin in 2026. CRYOSTAR (Università della Campania Luigi Vanvitelli) covers composite cryogenic liquid hydrogen tank structures and certification. LIME is led by Ascendance Flight Technologies. Consortium partners are published for each project.
research.why: EU consortia publish their full partner lists, which is a free map of who is doing funded composite structural work and with whom. CRYOSTAR is the one to read closely — cryogenic tank structures are a sandwich problem and the material selection is not yet frozen.

research.title: IFW realises complex composite sandwich structures with automated fibre placement
research.summary: Institute work on producing geometrically complex sandwich structures using automated fibre placement over core.
research.why: Directly relevant. AFP over core is exactly the production route that makes PMI attractive at rate — it needs a core that holds tolerance and survives the process. Worth approaching as a technical collaboration rather than a sale.

research.title: Thermoplastic sandwich structures for sustainable aircraft rudders
research.summary: Fraunhofer work on thermoplastic sandwich construction for aircraft rudders.
research.why: Read as a competitive warning rather than an opportunity. If thermoplastic sandwich becomes the default for control surfaces, PMI is designed out of a market it currently serves. Worth understanding the argument before a customer puts it to you.

research.title: Comparative analysis of sandwich composites with balsa, ROHACELL and Nomex cores for aerospace applications
research.summary: Head-to-head mechanical comparison of balsa, ROHACELL and Nomex honeycomb cores in aerospace sandwich construction.
research.why: Useful ammunition. A published, independent three-way comparison against the two incumbents you actually meet in the field is worth having read before a technical meeting — including knowing where it does not favour you.

research.title: US6107976 — Hybrid core sandwich radome
research.summary: Patent covering a radome built from a hybrid core sandwich construction.
research.why: Relevant to the open radome gap. Radome patents show how core is specified for dielectric rather than mechanical reasons, which is the argument PMI wins on. Old, so it is background reading rather than a lead.

research.title: CN104369387B — PMI foam sandwiched carbon fibre engineering truck boom
research.summary: PMI foam core in a carbon fibre composite boom for engineering vehicles.
research.why: Evidence that PMI already works in heavy moving machine structures, which supports the industrial and robotics case. Useful precedent to cite when that market is sceptical.

research.title: Rigid polymethacrylimide composite foam for electromagnetic dissipation and infrared stealth
research.summary: PMI foam engineered as a composite for electromagnetic wave dissipation and infrared signature reduction.
research.why: Potentially the most strategically interesting paper on this page. It moves PMI from being a structural core that happens to be RF-transparent to being a functional material for stealth and EM management. If that route matures it opens defence radome and signature-management work, which is exactly the gap you have in the Antennas and RF market. Worth reading in full before any defence conversation.

research.title: Lightweight, high-performance PMI foams for complex shapes from highly foamable precursor beads
research.summary: A bead-based foaming route that produces PMI in complex shapes rather than only in flat blocks and sheets.
research.why: Process research that matters commercially. Machining complex cores from block is slow and wasteful; a route to near-net shapes changes the cost argument in exactly the applications where PMI currently loses on price. Watch whether it reaches production.

research.title: Compressive behaviour and failure mechanism of PMI foam under thermo-mechanical coupling
research.summary: How PMI foam fails when temperature and mechanical load act together, with the underlying failure mechanisms identified.
research.why: Directly useful ammunition for the high-temperature argument you lead with at Destinus and other high-speed programmes. Independent data beats a datasheet in a technical meeting.

research.title: Compressive deformation of ROHACELL foams: effects of strain rate and temperature
research.summary: Strain-rate and temperature dependence of ROHACELL under compression.
research.why: The reference most often cited when someone asks how the material behaves under impact rather than static load. Worth having to hand for sports, automotive and any crash-relevant conversation.

research.title: Characterisation of the shear and compression failure envelope of ROHACELL foam
research.summary: Combined shear and compression failure envelope for ROHACELL.
research.why: Sandwich cores fail under combined loading, not pure compression. This is the data a structures engineer actually wants, and citing it signals you understand their problem rather than your product.

research.title: The mechanical response of ROHACELL foams at different length scales
research.summary: Behaviour of the foam from cell wall level up to bulk material.
research.why: Background reading. Useful when a customer asks why density and grade choice change behaviour so much.

research.title: ROHACELL foam for space applications
research.summary: Assessment of ROHACELL specifically for spacecraft structures.
research.why: Supporting material for the space market, where outgassing and thermal cycling are the questions that decide whether a core is allowed near a satellite.

research.title: NASA NTRS — Impact foam testing for Multi-Mission Earth Entry Vehicle applications
research.summary: NASA impact testing of foam materials for an Earth entry vehicle.
research.why: NASA NTRS is free, deep and fully searchable, and space agencies publish what industry keeps quiet. Worth mining as a standing source rather than a one-off.

research.title: NASA — Structural performance of a compressively loaded foam-core hat-stiffened composite panel
research.summary: Test data on a foam-cored stiffened composite panel under compression.
research.why: A rare published example of foam core used in a stiffened primary structure rather than a secondary panel. Useful precedent when an aerospace engineer assumes foam is only for lightly loaded parts.

research.title: Evonik expands ROHACELL production capacity in the US
research.summary: Capacity expansion for ROHACELL foams at the US site.
research.why: Commercially useful on a sales call. Lead time and security of supply are the two objections that kill core qualification, and a documented capacity expansion answers both. Know the numbers before someone asks whether you can supply at rate.

research.title: New German facility doubles ROHACELL production capacity
research.summary: German plant investment doubling ROHACELL output.
research.why: The European half of the same supply-security argument. Pair it with the US expansion when a customer worries about single-site risk.

research.title: PMI foam for aerospace — market size and forecast studies
research.summary: Commercial market sizing and forecasts for PMI foam in aerospace through the early 2030s.
research.why: Treat with caution — these reports are sold, not peer-reviewed, and the numbers vary wildly between houses. Useful only for the direction of travel and for internal business cases, never as evidence in a technical discussion.

They also stock Nomex honeycomb, so they will tell you honestly where each wins.

users.why: Their case-study library is the closest thing to a public reference list. Worth reading before a technical meeting — the applications they describe are ones already proven in service.

users.name: Avari Additive Manufacturing
users.what: Sells finished ROHACELL-core carbon fibre sandwich panels as a stock product.
users.why: Evidence of a finished-panel market: customers who want the sandwich, not the ingredients. A model worth understanding if any of your prospects would rather buy a panel than laminate one.

users.name: Bauer Hockey
users.what: Uses ROHACELL as the structural core in ice hockey stick blades. Evonik names them directly and describes the PMI foam as the core in the lower part of the stick.
users.why: Your cleanest consumer reference. The world’s largest producer of ice hockey sticks, named publicly, with the application described. Use it when a prospect doubts PMI survives real-world impact loading — a hockey blade takes worse abuse than most aerospace parts.

users.name: CarbonSports / Lightweight
users.what: Makes Lightweight-brand carbon racing wheel rims using a ROHACELL core, and has done since 2005. Rims come in under 1,000 grams.
users.why: A twenty-year reference in a brutally weight-obsessed market, and it is European. Two useful arguments come out of it: longevity of the material choice, and that professional cycling picked PMI over cheaper cores when grams genuinely decide races.

users.name: Dronamics
users.what: Uses ROHACELL in several key components of the Black Swan cargo drone. Their co-founder and CTO is quoted on structural integrity, durability and high-temperature performance.
users.why: The most commercially useful entry on this page. Dronamics is already tracked as a prospect — and they are not a prospect at all, they are an existing user. Change the approach accordingly: this is an expansion conversation about the new MALE variant, not a first qualification. A named CTO quote is also the strongest possible reference for other UAV makers.

users.name: SB Acoustics
users.what: Satori-range loudspeaker drivers built with carbon and ROHACELL sandwich cones. Widely discussed and sold through specialist audio retailers.
users.why: Audio is a market that barely appears in composite trade press but buys real volume. A cone is a thin, stiff, low-mass sandwich — exactly PMI territory. Worth understanding as a proof point, and as a hint that other driver manufacturers are candidates.

users.name: Clarasonic
users.what: Listed under ROHACELL in the Loudspeaker Industry Sourcebook as a speaker component manufacturer.
users.why: Second independent signal that PMI has an established position in loudspeaker cones. Outside your territory, but it corroborates the audio application rather than resting on one forum thread.

users.name: Smartphone speaker membranes
users.what: Ultra-thin ROHACELL grades developed for smartphone speaker membranes.
users.why: Logged as an application rather than a company, because the handset makers do not name their suppliers. Useful mainly as evidence of how thin the material can be processed, which surprises people who only know it as a 10mm aerospace core.

users.name: Unicamp E-Racing / FSAE Unicamp
users.what: Formula SAE team of roughly 100 students. ROHACELL PMI is the core in the aerodynamic package of their E2021 car — front wing, rear wing and endplates. Confirmed by Evonik and posted by the team on Instagram.
users.why: This corrects an earlier gap. The first sweep found no Formula Student team using ROHACELL and concluded student teams were an untapped opportunity. They are not — at least one is a confirmed user, and Evonik supported it publicly. Student teams are cheap to support, they publish everything they build, and the engineers graduate into exactly the companies on your target list. Treat this as a template worth repeating with European teams.

users.name: AMT Composites
users.what: Distributor posting publicly about supplying ROHACELL IG-F as a structural foam core.
users.why: Channel outside Europe, found via an indexed Instagram post rather than any trade source — a good illustration that social posts surface distributors who never appear in the composites press.

users.name: Epic Fibers
users.what: Sells carbon fibre / ROHACELL PMI sandwich panels as a standard product line alongside honeycomb and PVC cored panels.
users.why: Another finished-panel supplier. Useful for prospects who would rather buy a panel than laminate one, and their honeycomb-versus-PMI product range tells you how they position the two against each other.

users.name: Composite Envisions (CST Sales)
users.what: Stocks carbon fibre ROHACELL sandwich panels.
users.why: US finished-panel channel. Same pattern as Epic Fibers — evidence that a ready-made PMI panel market exists and is worth understanding before a prospect asks whether they can just buy the sandwich.

users_note:
This list is anyone publicly on record using, converting, stocking or distributing ROHACELL, in any industry and any country — end products first, then converters and channel, with the strongest evidence at the top.

How these are found: trade press, Evonik’s own customer stories, distributor listings, technical forums, and indexed social posts. Instagram hashtag pages cannot be browsed directly — they are behind a login — but individual posts do get indexed by search engines, and that is how the Unicamp Formula SAE team and AMT Composites were found. The daily scan searches that way deliberately.

Standing caveat: OEMs almost never name their core supplier, and F1 teams disclose nothing at all about materials. Absence from this list is weak evidence of absence.

shows.name: DroneX Trade Show & Conference
shows.what: The UK's largest dedicated drone event, covering commercial and defence unmanned systems.
shows.why: The nearest show and the one this list should have had from the start. Six weeks away, in London, and it is squarely your top market. UK UAV makers and their suppliers in one hall — and the sort of event where the smaller airframe builders actually turn up rather than sending a brochure.
shows.todo: Get the exhibitor list now and cross-check it against the tracked UAV companies. Six weeks is enough to book meetings properly.

shows.name: InnoTrans
shows.what: The world’s largest rail technology trade fair, including interiors and vehicle structures.
shows.why: Only worth going if you are serious about rail, and remember the gate there is EN 45545 fire certification rather than mechanical performance. Turning up without FST data wastes the trip. Listed for completeness, not recommended as a priority.
shows.todo: Skip unless the rail FST data package is ready. If it is, this is the one rail show that matters.

shows.name: Advanced Engineering UK
shows.what: The UK's largest advanced manufacturing show, with a composites zone and the co-located Advanced Materials Show.
shows.why: Broad but genuinely useful: UK composite fabricators, tier suppliers and airframe makers together. Several tracked companies exhibit — Dash-CAE, Permali, SHD and Callen-Lenz territory — so it is four trips collapsed into two days.
shows.todo: Cross-check the exhibitor list against the tracked list when it publishes. Book meetings before the show, not on the day.

shows.name: Space Tech Expo Europe
shows.what: Europe's largest business-to-business space event — satellite primes, smallsat makers, launchers and supply chain.
shows.why: Highest-value show for your strongest new market. Satellite structures are almost entirely sandwich panel, and this puts the whole European supply chain in one place. EnduroSat and Aerospacelab territory. Two weeks after Advanced Engineering, so plan both together.
shows.todo: Prioritise smallsat manufacturers and structure suppliers over the primes — the primes already have locked supply chains.

shows.name: METSTRADE
shows.what: The largest marine equipment trade show in the world.
shows.why: Low priority and worth being honest about why: Gurit’s SAN foam owns the marine core market on price and toughness. Only useful if you are specifically chasing high-performance racing yachts or lightweight fast ferries, where stiffness per kilo justifies the premium.
shows.todo: Skip unless a specific high-performance marine lead has already emerged.

shows.name: JEC World
shows.what: The leading international composites show. Every core supplier, prepregger, fabricator and OEM materials team attends.
shows.why: The densest gathering of your market anywhere. Also where every competitor will be — Gurit, Diab, Armacell, the honeycomb makers — which makes it as valuable for positioning intelligence as for leads. Long lead time, so plan it properly rather than turning up.
shows.todo: Build the target list over the winter from tracked companies, then book meetings early. The good slots go months ahead.

shows.name: AERO Friedrichshafen
shows.what: The global general aviation trade show — light aircraft, gliders, electric and hydrogen propulsion.
shows.why: Good fit for the certified aircraft and interiors market, and gliders and light airframes are a traditional PMI application. Smaller manufacturers who are reachable, rather than primes who are not.
shows.todo: Worth a scouting visit before committing to a stand. Look for electric and hydrogen light aircraft programmes still in design.

shows.name: Eurosatory
shows.when: June, biennial — next edition to confirm
shows.what: One of the largest land and airland defence exhibitions in the world.
shows.why: Defence UAS and loitering munition makers in volume. Worth tracking given how much of your top market is now defence-funded, but confirm the next edition before planning.
shows.todo: Confirm the next edition date. Cross-check against the defence UAS companies tracked.

shows.name: DSEI London
shows.what: The UK’s largest defence and security exhibition.
shows.why: UK defence procurement in one place, and the UK is spending heavily on drones. Biennial, so the next edition is 2027 — long lead time but worth diarising.
shows.todo: Confirm dates when the organiser publishes. Lower priority than DroneX for reaching airframe builders directly.

shows.name: ISPO Munich
shows.what: The leading international sports business trade show — ski, outdoor, cycling, equipment brands.
shows.why: The sports market is fragmented and largely Asian-manufactured, so this is a low-yield show for direct leads. Its value is spotting brands announcing European manufacturing, which is the signal worth acting on in that sector.
shows.todo: Low priority. Watch the exhibitor list remotely rather than attending.

shows.name: COMPAMED / MEDICA
shows.what: The leading trade fair for medical device component suppliers, alongside MEDICA.
shows.why: Where the tier suppliers who actually build imaging tables and covers exhibit — which is the right level to target, since the OEMs rarely specify core themselves. Radiolucent PMI is already incumbent here, so this is about defending and extending.
shows.todo: Target component manufacturers and contract builders, not the imaging OEMs.

shows.name: Professional MotorSport World Expo
shows.what: Motorsport engineering and technology suppliers, co-located with related automotive expos.
shows.why: Motorsport composite fabricators and tub builders in one place. Smaller and more technical than a general automotive show, which suits a core material conversation.
shows.todo: Confirm dates. Good pairing with Advanced Engineering in the same month.

shows_note:
Every show relevant to the nine markets, nearest first. Confirmed means the dates come from the organiser or venue; Dates to confirm means the event is real but the exact dates still need checking — treat those as diary placeholders, not bookings.

Exhibitor lists are one of the few genuinely pre-qualified target lists available free: a company paying for a stand is by definition active in that market, and lists publish months ahead. The daily scan watches for them and cross-checks against the tracked companies.

Not every show here is worth attending, and the notes say so plainly — METSTRADE and ISPO are listed mainly so you can see they were considered and why they rank low.
